input:
This executive summary considers a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and asks whether the project should proceed at this stage. The recommendation is that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, with the plant engineer owning the trial.

By way of background, the plant currently uses 2234 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which represents a substantial part of the site's overall energy picture. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 11% of that electricity use, which works out to a derived saving of 246 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $414k. Using an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.8 years, a payback period that is long in relation to the amount of capital that would be put at risk.

It is important to note, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and that the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, which means that the annual figures rest on assumptions that have yet to be tested against the plant's actual behaviour. A metered trial would help to address this uncertainty by generating measured evidence on one line, allowing a more robust decision to be made before the full capital commitment is entered into.
target:
The recommendation is a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.

The plant uses 2234 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 11% of that use, a derived saving of 246 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $414k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.8 years. On the vendor figure alone, the payback is long relative to the sum at risk, and the figure carries the whole case: every derived quantity in the summary traces back to the projected percentage.

The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the annual projection also rests on a load profile that the peak month may not follow. A metered trial on one line replaces the projected percentage with a measured one for that line, at the cost of metering rather than the cost of the retrofit. The capital decision then rests on a saving measured at this plant, on a line whose load the trial records, and the payback can be recomputed from measured quantities before the full capital cost is committed. The trial also bounds the commitment in scope: one line is metered, the other lines continue as they are, and the retrofit decision waits for the trial result instead of running ahead of it. What the trial cannot settle is the summer peak, whose load was not modelled; how the peak month is handled has to be stated before the trial begins.
